planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once frost danger has passed, in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; give it room to sucker and self-seed since it can wander further than most garden cestrums.

directions: Native to Chile and Argentina, willow-leaved jessamine is a fast-growing, semi-deciduous shrub with narrow lance-shaped leaves and loose clusters of yellow-green tubular flowers that release a strong, sweet fragrance only after dark. It dies back to woody stems in a hard freeze but resprouts readily from the base in zone 8b and warmer, and benefits from an annual hard pruning to keep its lax habit tidy and to limit self-seeding, which can become a nuisance in mild climates. Every part of this plant is significantly more toxic than related cestrums, containing liver-damaging alkaloids that have caused fatal poisonings in grazing livestock, so it should be sited well away from pastures, pets, and children. Choose a planting spot with good air movement, since the strongest scent carries best on still summer evenings.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring after frost danger has passed, in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in a sheltered site with morning sun and afternoon shade in the hottest parts of zone 9-10.

directions: This RHS Award of Garden Merit cultivar produces dense, drooping clusters of scarlet-red tubular flowers over a long season, followed by reddish-purple berries, and carries a sweet perfume that becomes noticeable as temperatures drop toward evening rather than being purely nocturnal like night-blooming jessamine. It grows into a semi-evergreen, upright-arching shrub that is a reliable hummingbird and butterfly magnet, and it tolerates being cut back hard each late winter to renew flowering wood and control its size. Give it a sheltered spot against a wall or under high canopy in the cooler parts of its range, since foliage and stems can be damaged by prolonged hard freezes even though the root system generally survives. As with all cestrums, the berries are toxic if eaten and should be kept away from children and pets.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed, in fertile, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; give it plenty of room since it grows into a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree in frost-free years.

directions: Recent botanical revisions place this Brazilian Atlantic Forest species under the genus Pleroma, but it remains widely sold in the trade as Tibouchina mutabilis. Its Latin name references its most distinctive trait: individual flowers open white, then age through pink to deep magenta, so a single plant can display all three colors simultaneously across its bloom clusters for most of the warm season. It grows considerably larger and more tree-like than the common princess flower and needs full sun to flower and color-shift at its best, along with an acidic, well-drained soil similar to what azaleas prefer. Where winter cold cuts it to the ground, it typically resprouts vigorously from the woody base once the soil warms in spring.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed, in fertile, acidic, moisture-retentive soil with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the oversized leaves from scorching.

directions: This Brazilian native, once favored by landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx, is grown chiefly for its enormous, velvety, felt-textured leaves that can span nearly ten inches across on an otherwise typically shaped rounded shrub. Upright terminal clusters of royal-purple flowers appear from fall into winter, later in the season than most other landscape tibouchinas, giving cool-season interest when little else in the genus is blooming. The huge leaves are more prone to wind tatter and sunscald than smaller-leaved relatives like princess flower, so a site with midday or afternoon shade and shelter from strong wind keeps the foliage looking its best. Feed with an acidic fertilizer formulated for camellias or azaleas and protect from hard freezes, since both foliage and stems are damaged well before temperatures approach freezing.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed, in slightly acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter; this selection stays more compact than seed-grown princess flower while carrying noticeably larger blooms.

directions: Selected for unusually large, three-inch royal-purple flowers crowning velvety, red-edged foliage, 'Edwardsii' is a named cultivar of the standard princess flower that keeps to a tighter, more rounded frame than seed-grown plants of the species. It blooms most heavily from late summer through fall but will flower intermittently year-round in the warmest, sunniest microclimates of coastal zone 9 to 10 gardens. Give it morning sun with some afternoon relief in peak summer heat, and mulch well since it prefers consistent moisture over drought. Unlike the University of Georgia-bred 'Athens Blue' selection, which was chosen mainly for compactness and floriferousness, 'Edwardsii' is prized primarily for its oversized individual blossoms.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once nights stay reliably warm, in humus-rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in dappled shade; grow in a large container with winter protection outside the warmest parts of zone 10-11.

directions: Sold under the synonym Brunfelsia hopeana, manaca is native to rainforest understory from Trinidad and Venezuela through Brazil, where indigenous communities have long used it medicinally despite its considerable toxicity. Its intensely fragrant, yellowish-white flowers open with a faint violet tinge and fade to pure white over a few days, echoing the color-change pattern of its better-known relative yesterday-today-tomorrow, with peak fragrance building through the evening. It performs best in warm, humid, sheltered shade with steady moisture and protection from any direct hot afternoon sun, which can scorch its broad leaves. Every part of the plant, including the berries, is toxic if ingested and has caused severe poisoning, tremors, and seizures in dogs, so it must be kept well out of reach of pets and children.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring after frost danger passes, in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this selection tolerates drier, shadier sites than the blue-flowered Cape plumbago.

directions: 'Summer Snow' is a named selection of the pantropical native white plumbago, sometimes still labeled under its older name Plumbago scandens, chosen in the nursery trade for a heavier, more consistent flush of white bloom through the hottest months than typical seed-grown plants. It forms a sprawling, semi-scandent mound of glossy narrow foliage that flowers well even in fairly deep shade, making it a useful filler for dry, shaded borders where few other flowering shrubs perform reliably. It serves as a larval host plant for the cassius blue butterfly and needs little supplemental water once established, though hard freezes will kill it back to the crown in the cooler parts of its range. Wear gloves when pruning, since the stem sap can irritate sensitive skin.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions
